 Dan Koh says challenging House speaker would slow Democrats' progress 
 Morning Edition 
 Share
 Email 
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 Congressman-elect Dan Koh represents Massachusetts' 6th congressional district. 
 Nathan Howard
 AP
 Tori Bedford
 tori_bedford 
 victoria.bedford@gbh.org 
 Tori Bedford hosts evening newscasts on GBH radio and reports for GBH News. Feedback? Questions? Story ideas? Reach out to Tori at tori.bedford@gbh.org. 
 November 16, 2026
 Congressman-elect Dan Koh will represent Massachusetts’ 6th congressional district as the first Asian American and Arab American to represent Massachusetts when he takes office in January. 
 He spoke with GBH Morning Edition’s Tori Bedford about the new class of Democrats heading to Congress and their plans for the future. What follows is a lightly edited transcript. 
 Tori Bedford: So, congratulations on the win. This is your second run for a seat in Congress. You stuck with it. It worked out. How are you feeling? How’s orientation?

 Dan Koh: It’s been a very humbling but honorable experience just to be among so many incredible people who flipped districts all across this country. Sam Forstag from Montana, the former smokejumper. Denise Powell from Nebraska. I mean, these are just all people who have gone through the wringer the last year plus, and it’s just an honor to serve with them. Most importantly, to represent the amazing people of the 6th district and be able to actually lower costs and take this president on.
 Bedford: Yeah, this was an incredible election. You mentioned so many progressive candidates. There’s a group of incoming Democrats that have been dubbed the Bloc, following in the path of the Squad, but differentiated from the Squad. You’ve been named among those newcomers. Do you consider yourself a part of the Bloc, this group of progressive Dems?
 Koh: I consider myself a part of any group that wants to stop the grift of this president and actually deliver government that works for people. And that sounds kind of cliché, but the reality is we have every single day a president who’s more interested in spending taxpayer dollars on ballrooms, and defunding things like investigating the outcomes of firefighters when they die in the line of duty. And that’s really something that I think every American should be concerned about. And I used to work in government. I’ve seen how good government can work for people. And I think we need to get back to that.
 Bedford: Yeah, you spent 2 and a half years working in the Biden-Harris administration. You served as Chief of Staff to U.S. Labor Secretary Marty Walsh. Those are some, I think, could be perceived as establishment credentials, as compared to like a wildland firefighter and smokejumper — you mentioned Forstag. How do you plan to navigate that and work with this new progressive class?
 Koh: I think I feel pretty good if a Korean Lebanese guy who was a town selectman in Andover is considered the establishment. So, you know, I think we have a lot of progress we need to make as a collective group of folks. And I’m proud of the time that I served in the administration. And I think, you know, anyone coming from a new perspective like I am, coming from different backgrounds, is good. The collective group of people here who are looking to really take on this president and actually make government a force for people to believe in again is something that I’m just really honored to be a part of.
 Bedford: You talked about your desire to hold the Trump administration accountable for crimes, lowering costs. But, you know, there’ are also so many issues, everyday issues facing Americans. Can you walk and chew gum at the same time?

 Koh: Well, I think we have to. I think, first and foremost, every American here is dealing with a million different priorities at once. I’m the dad of a 6- and a 3-year-old, and you never have a choice between choosing between one or the other if one is sick or one’s got a wet diaper or something like that. And so, I don’t think that government officials should have the luxury of choosing one or the other. I also think it’s a false choice between accountability and affordability. If we hold this president accountable and end the war in Iran — which is illegal, has cost us $50 billion and Congress has not exercised their coequal constitutional duty to check [the president] — prices will go down fundamentally. At the very least, gas prices, your gas prices as well as diesel fuel, which will bring down the cost of groceries. So, I think we need to do both. We need to do it fast. People did not elect me to sit around. They elected me to work hard before day one, and that’s exactly what I’m doing.
 Bedford: The war in Iran is a priority of the Democrats in this Congress. But what do you think the future relationship should be with the U.S. and Israel? Do you plan to vote on continuing to send military funding and weapons to Israel?
 Koh: I think that Benjamin Netanyahu has done a disservice to the state of Israel, who has formerly been an ally of ours, with the actions that have happened in Gaza and, candidly, the actions of a number of different things in the Middle East. And so, you know, I think that everything needs to be on the table. And I think that what we have seen in America with Donald Trump, what I really hope, to be honest, is that we don’t hold all Israelis accountable for what Netanyahu has done in the same way that we should not hold all Americans accountable for the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu. But I think we need to be very concerned that all aid and everything that we do as Americans and the alliances that we have are all in accordance with international law and Leahy laws. And I do not believe that that has always been the case with Israel.
 Bedford: Okay. You spoke to our colleagues Jim and Margery on Boston Public Radio. You said you do support Hakeem Jeffries as Speaker of the House. But my interpretation was that you seem to have left the door open by also noting that he’s the only choice right now. As you know, in the Senate, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Senator Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader. There’s this online petition supporting a potential challenge to Hakeem Jeffries as Speaker from your colleague, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley. It’s got about 144,000 signatures. If Pressley were to challenge Jeffries, where would you stand?
 Koh: I won’t operate in hypotheticals. I think I have a ton of respect for Congresswoman Pressley. I think Congresswoman Pressley would be a great speaker. But I’m not going to operate in hypotheticals because she is not currently a candidate for Speaker of the House. I’ve spoken to Leader Jeffries. He is very aware of some of the concerns that people have, including members of the freshman class, about where we need to go as an administration. And I think that one other thing that is important to note is that there was nothing that made me happier when I worked in the White House than seeing the amount of discord that happened with the Kevin McCarthy speaker battle that cost Republicans valuable time to enact their agenda. We have less than two years. I would argue we have two to three months max to prove to the American people that their faith in new leadership in government can and should be rewarded with bold legislation, like Medicare for All, restoring Medicare and Medicaid cuts, making sure that people have access to their SNAP benefits. We can’t blow it. And I worry that a big speaker fight would blow it.
 Bedford: President Trump has threatened to veto anything that Democrats try to get done. Do you think he’ll be able to derail much of the party’s plans?
 Koh: I would be ecstatic if for the next few months he tried to veto the kind of legislation that Americans have been clamoring for, for more than a decade. Stock trading bans should be enacted on day one, for example. I want him to veto that. Let him veto that and let the American people see that the only doorstop to progress in this country is the presidency. It would make a very easy path for a Democrat to win in 2028. 
 I think what’s going to happen is that he’s going to have no choice but to allow the legislation to pass because things like the Medicaid and Medicare cuts, as well as the SNAP benefits that have been enacted, disproportionately affect red states. The people who did win, who are Republican this cycle, many of them barely hung on to their seats. They are not going to want to be associated with a lame duck president with a 30% approval rating if they want to get reelected. So, I think there’s a real opportunity for Democrats to really enact true change as a result.
 Tori Bedford
 tori_bedford
